definition: A system approximating the interactive or behavioural intelligence of a species; in this course it also reaches beyond machine learning to include symbolic systems, search and planning that involve no learning at all.
A system that captures the underlying probability distribution of a dataset in order to synthesise new samples that appear to originate from that same distribution.
Human-level breadth of intelligence across every task a person can do. The G is General, not Generative, and AGI is explicitly out of scope for this course.
AI judged on accuracy against verifiable ground truths; it asks 'what will be?', learning a mapping x to y that you then crank by supplying new inputs.

Turing's 1950 test: if the quality of interaction is so human-like that you cannot tell machine from person, the question of whether it thinks is set aside. It tests only the human-like sense of intelligence, not correctness.
'Intelligence' in the sense of extracted information of tactical or strategic value — the same sense as military intelligence, and not the sense used in 'AI'.
'Intelligence' in the sense of an optimal solution path or method for a complex problem, as in digital or computational intelligence.
The first sense of the A in AI: a machine creation made by humans rather than found in nature. True of every AI system, so it never distinguishes one case from another.
The second sense of the A in AI: the standard by which 'seems about right' will do — the standard a generated image is held to.
The third sense of the A in AI: 'truth manufactured', shaped by whatever is trending.
Unpacked three ways in this course: simulate (draw from a distributional prior), connect (graph or network adjacency), and create (integrated innovation).
What generation is: a mapping into territory never explicitly observed, which is why it is called imagination rather than validation.
A known correct answer against which a prediction can be scored. Predictive AI is evaluated against these; generative AI has none, which is why it is judged differently.
The standard generative AI is judged by: whether the output is convincing and relevant to its context, since there is no ground truth for something newly invented.
Programming a system to calibrate its model parameters from data rather than writing if-then rules by hand. Its methods reach far outside AI, into statistics, optimisation and forecasting.
Learning from labelled targets by error correction — the paradigm behind an MLP classifier.
Learning structure from data with no labels supplied, as cluster analysis does.
Learning a policy by optimising against a reward signal rather than against labelled answers.
Nacaskul's five-element framework: corporal form, valenced feeling, cognitive faculty, mental formation, and consciousness marker.

The second element of the Intelligent Being: grading sensed input on a preferential scale from very negative through neutral to very positive, which acts as feedback to the learning algorithm and conditions future behaviour.
The first element of the Intelligent Being: a physical body with sensors and some autonomy, letting the agent interactively explore and learn from its environment.
The third element of the Intelligent Being: learning an internal model of reality, forming memory, classifying and predicting — hence predictive AI.
The fourth element of the Intelligent Being: generatively imagining realistic scenarios, shapes and ideas — hence generative AI.
The fifth element of the Intelligent Being: momentary, sequential awareness of the computation step being performed, and the hook for the machine-consciousness debate.
Appreciating how AI got where it is, how it is trained from data, and both the capability and the pitfalls of AI solutions — so as not to apply AI blindly.
The failure mode of AI literacy: outsourcing your essay, your pitch and your reading to a chatbot, so the competence never forms.
Designing an innovation to work within an integrated reality — not the integration of impressive features bolted together.
Working under real-world constraints rather than simplified ones, which is why applied mathematics is harder than theoretical mathematics, not easier.
Learning p(y given x) — the probability of a label given an input. The predictive side of the arc.
Learning p(x), or p(x given a condition c) — the distribution of the data itself, so that new samples can be drawn from it.

Pulling a generality out of specific experiences so it can be applied to new situations. Animals do it adaptively, humans deliberately, and AI at scale — 'AI did not invent abstraction; it industrialized it'.
Turing's 1950 paper, which opens the language-AI timeline and introduces the imitation game.
The 1956 summer workshop at Dartmouth College generally treated as the founding of AI as an academic field.
Rule-based formal logic over symbols: hand-written if-then rules, no learning from data. The dominant approach from the 1950s until the neural revival.
Good Old-Fashioned AI — the retronym applied to symbolic, rule-based AI once neural approaches took the name 'AI' for themselves.
A new name for an older thing, coined because a newer thing took the original name. Expert systems became 'GOFAI'; ordinary AI became 'predictive AI'.
A rule-based program encoding a specialist's knowledge as if-then rules, from about 1965; early success in medical diagnosis.
A 1975 expert system that diagnosed bacterial infections at about 65% accuracy — the standard example of what rule-based AI could and could not do.
The two programming languages associated with the symbolic-AI era and with expert systems.
The Canadian system that from 1981 translated weather reports between English and French — early natural-language processing that actually shipped.
IBM's chess program, which beat the world champion in 1997 using search and hand-built evaluation rather than learning from data.
Mikolov's 2013 method for turning English words into vectors of numbers, trained by guessing a missing word from its neighbours. It made word algebra possible and made words usable as network input.
Vaswani and colleagues' 2017 paper introducing the Transformer, and the source of the T in GPT. The title's claim is that recurrence and convolution can be dropped entirely.
The 1943 mathematical model of a neuron, which opens the neurocomputational thread.
The claim that the brain has no central processor — it is just neurons connected to neurons — so intelligence should be built by replicating that mechanism rather than the outward behaviour.
The actual brain: nerve cells connected in a network, passing stimulus between them.
A mathematical model of a biological neural network. Every modern AI system is built from ANNs.
The researchers who, around 1959, recorded from a cat's striate cortex and found neurons that fired for oriented lines rather than for whole objects — the finding the CNN is built on.
Fukushima's 1980 network, the first convolutional architecture and the direct descendant of the cat experiment.
LeCun's 1998 convolutional network, which cracked handwritten character recognition.
The large labelled image dataset built from 2010 by Fei-Fei Li — the missing ingredient that made deep vision models trainable.
Krizhevsky, Sutskever and Hinton's 2012 convolutional network, which cut ImageNet error from about 25% to single digits and started the deep-learning era in vision.
Their 1969 result showed a single perceptron cannot learn XOR, which stalled neural research until multi-layer networks and backpropagation arrived.
A mathematical-computational model of a generic neuron: it sums weighted incoming signals, excitatory or inhibitory, and fires if the sum exceeds an internal threshold.
Feedforward layers of perceptrons stacked, each layer's output becoming the next layer's input. No recurrence and no skipping layers.
A network in which the signal travels one way only, from input towards output.
A network in which the signal loops back, so earlier outputs feed later computation.
A learned number scaling one input to a neuron. Weight, coefficient and parameter all mean the same thing in this course.
The learned number added to a neuron's weighted sum, which shifts its decision threshold — as opposed to the weights, which scale the inputs.
A number learned from data during training, as opposed to an input you supply or a hyperparameter you set beforehand.
A setting fixed before training begins — layer sizes, learning rate — rather than learned from the data.
Choosing which x variables to feed the model, given what you want to predict and what your data contains.
Building a new input from existing ones by a logical function, such as dividing one variable by another, before the data reaches the model.
The nonlinearity applied to a neuron's weighted sum. Without it, stacking layers gains nothing, because a chain of linear maps is still linear.
An activation that squashes any real input into the range 0 to 1. It suffers from vanishing gradients in deep networks, which is why ReLU displaced it.
The rectified linear unit, or ramp: returns its input if positive and zero otherwise. A cheap nonlinearity and the modern default.
Converts a vector of raw activations into a probability distribution over classes, summing to one. Sigmoid squashes a single value; softmax works across a whole vector.
Data that a single straight boundary can divide correctly. A single perceptron can only handle this case, which is why XOR requires layers.
The classic counterexample to the single perceptron: no one straight line separates the true cases from the false ones, so layers are needed.
A single number measuring how far the network's output is from the target. Training minimises it.
Root Mean Squared Error — one specific loss function, natural when the target is a quantity. The loss is the general idea; RMSE is an instance of it.
The vector giving the direction of steepest ascent of the loss. Training steps against it.
The iterative, stepwise optimiser: from wherever you are, find the direction that reduces the loss fastest, take a small step, and repeat.

A specialisation of the gradient descent algorithm, applied to minimise prediction error for a multilayer perceptron by tweaking its weights and biases, sending the error backwards through the layers.
Adaptive Moment Estimation — a refinement of plain gradient descent that adapts the size of each step.
A representation in which exactly one slot is on and all the rest are off — the standard output format for a classifier over a fixed set of classes.

The result that a network with a single hidden layer and finitely many neurons can approximate any continuous function on a closed bounded region to any tolerance. It establishes representational capacity only: it does not promise that training will find the parameters, or that the result will generalise.
Neural networks with many layers, trained end to end. Not a new architecture but the multilayer perceptron idea at depth and scale.
Training error continues to fall while validation error plateaus or rises — the model is learning the training set rather than the pattern.
Both training and validation error stay high: the model lacks the capacity or the training to capture the pattern at all.
A network built from convolutional layers, designed for grid-structured data such as images by exploiting locality and weight sharing.
A layer of convolution matrices with trainable entries, slid across a grid of pixel values to detect underlying visual patterns.
Applying the same learned filter at every position in the image, so a feature is detected wherever it appears and the parameter count does not grow with image size.
The network processes every region with the same learned filters, so features are detected consistently across locations.
Handling the same object at different apparent sizes, because distance from the camera changes how large it appears.
The property that the predicted label does not change when the input is rotated — though symmetry sometimes matters, since flipping 'bp' gives 'qd'.
Small features combining into larger ones: edges into shapes into objects, leaves into trees into forest. Borrowed directly from the cat's visual cortex.
The tendency of neighbouring pixels in natural images to have similar colours, with the similarity falling off as distance grows.
The brain's binding of spatially aligned features into a single perceived object; one of the vision principles CNN design borrows.
A layer that reduces the size of the representation, summarising each small neighbourhood into a single value.
Converting the three-dimensional tensor produced by the convolutional stack into a one-dimensional vector that fully-connected layers can consume.
The multi-dimensional array that a network's numbers live in.
The component that converts raw image data into the normalised numeric arrays a neural network can take as input.
The distance between the predicted class probabilities and the true one-hot encoded label — the natural loss when the target is a class rather than a quantity.
Randomly switching off a fraction of units during training so the network cannot rely on any single path; a regulariser against overfitting.
Manufacturing extra plausible training examples by flipping or slightly translating the originals, forcing the model to generalise.
The region of the input image a given neuron can actually see. It widens with depth, which is why early layers detect edges and deep layers detect objects.
A map showing which input pixels most affect a given output for a particular image — measurement, as opposed to the receptive field, which is architecture.
A network trained to reproduce its own input after forcing it through a narrow middle layer. It needs no labels, because the target is the input itself.
The narrow middle layer of an autoencoder, holding fewer numbers than the input, which forces the network to discard accidents and keep structure.
The compressed internal representation at an autoencoder's bottleneck, in which each point stands for an input and nearby points stand for similar inputs.
An autoencoder whose encoder outputs a probability distribution over the latent space rather than a single point, so a new point can be sampled and decoded into a new, realistic example.
An architecture that compresses the input into a representation and then expands that representation into the target — which may be the input, a translation of it, or a mask over it.
The half of an autoencoder that turns a latent code back into data. Once the latent space is one you can sample from, the decoder is the generator.
An encoder-decoder CNN with skip connections carrying fine spatial detail across the bottleneck; used for segmentation, reconstruction and medical imaging.
A direct link from an encoder stage to the matching decoder stage, restoring the fine detail that downsampling destroyed. It is what gives the U-Net its shape.
Representing data with fewer numbers while keeping what matters. An autoencoder does it by learning, rather than by a fixed rule.
Spotting unusual inputs by their reconstruction error: an autoencoder trained on normal examples reconstructs them well and everything else badly.
The half of a VAE's objective that keeps the decoded output close to the original input, balanced against latent regularisation.
The middle stage of the six-architecture arc — VAE and U-Net — which learns compact structured representations and so serves both prediction and generation.
The 2017 architecture built from token embeddings, positional encoding, self-attention layers and feedforward blocks, with no recurrence and no convolution.
The unit a sentence is chopped into before embedding — usually a word or a fragment of one, drawn from a fixed vocabulary.
The learned vector that carries an item's meaning, in which similar items sit close together. It supplies global-context meaning, as against attention's local-context interpretation.
The property that directions in embedding space correspond to consistent relationships, so king minus male plus female lands near queen.
The mechanism that weighs how much every other token should inform each token's interpretation, supplying local context within the particular sentence.
Attention in which queries, keys and values all come from the same sequence: every token weighing every other token in its own sentence.
The three roles attention is built from: the query is what a token is looking for, the key is what each other token offers, and the value is the content passed along when they match.
Information added to each token's vector recording where it sits in the sequence, since attention itself is order-blind.

Generative Pre-trained Transformer: generative because it produces new text, pre-trained because it learns from an internet-scale corpus before any task, transformer because attention weighs every other token.
A very large transformer pre-trained on internet-scale text to predict the next token, then used to generate language.
Two networks in a minimax game: a generator makes fakes and a discriminator judges real against fake, each improving as the other does. Goodfellow and colleagues, 2014.
The half of a GAN that produces fakes from random input, learning only from how well it fools the discriminator.
The half of a GAN that judges real against fake — an ordinary predictive classifier, and the only training signal the generator gets.
A convincing fake video or image of a real person produced by generative models; the application that made adversarial networks famous.
A model that learns to reverse a fixed noising process, so generation starts from pure noise and iteratively denoises into data.
In a diffusion model, the prescribed step-by-step corruption of data with Gaussian noise. It is designed rather than learned, which is what makes the reverse a supervised problem.
Defining a probability path from a simple distribution to the data and learning the vector field that transports samples along it; generation means starting from noise and following the learned flow.
Steering a generative model with extra input, such as a text embedding consulted at every denoising step of a text-to-image model.
The low-dimensional, structured surface that real data occupy within the space of all possible values — the assumption that makes a mapping from a simple distribution possible at all.
The pseudo-random number generator you 'crank' to produce a new sample: the randomness supplies variation while the learned mapping supplies structure.
An adversarial architecture for unpaired image-to-image translation, learning a mapping between two image collections with no matched example pairs.
MLP, CNN, VAE, U-Net, Transformer and Diffusion — predictive, representation bridge, then generative.

term: Five principles of modern deep learning
definition: Representation, Relation, Parameterization, Optimization, Architecture — represent, relate, parameterize, learn, orchestrate. Not ever more complicated primitive mathematics, but increasingly ingenious orchestration of representations, relationships, parameters and learning.
Low-value, mass-produced AI-generated content flooding the web, cheap enough to produce that its volume swamps material worth reading.
Handing thinking work to an external tool. Offloading the reasoning itself is the risky case, because the judgement needed to check the answer never develops.
The population-level effect of everyone offloading their reasoning: critical thinking weakens at the same rate answers become easier to get.
A fluent invention stated as fact by a generative model — the direct consequence of optimising for plausible context relevance rather than for accuracy.
A model reproducing the bias in its training data, because parameters are calibrated from a record of what people did rather than of what was right.
The loop in which machine-generated content fills the corpus that future models train on, so distortions are amplified rather than corrected.
Retrieval-Augmented Generation: retrieve relevant documents first, then generate grounded on them, for factual verifiability. Mapped to the term project rather than this exam.
The first principle: encode task-relevant information as vectors or tensors so that it becomes computable. Tokens and embeddings for text, patches and tensors for images.
The second principle: express abstract relationships as algebraic or geometric operations among representations. Attention, with its query, key and value, is the textbook example.
The third principle: simple operations, massively parameterised and composed, can express complex functions. Complexity is bought with learned parameters, not with exotic mathematics.
The fourth principle: make the system differentiable so its numerical parameters can be learned from data by gradient-based methods.
The fifth principle: the higher-level design that orchestrates the other four, deciding how representations, relations, parameterised operations and learning interact.
The course's own four-stage map: Words Matter (build the language), Timelines (how we got here), HIWUTH (how it works under the hood), Application (what you can do with it).

The timeline family tracking the reproduction of human capabilities — language, vision, problem solving, decision making — from Turing 1950 through expert systems and deep learning to large language models.
The timeline family tracking competing conceptions of intelligence: symbolic/logical, neurocomputational, statistical/data-driven and hybrid.
The timeline family running from AI as software, through AI as an operating system (agentic AI: reasoning, planning, tool use), to AI as hardware (robotics and embodied AI).

A physical agent acting in the world, described with five elements: physical form, valenced sensing, cognition function (predictive intelligence), concept formation (generative intelligence) and experience register.

The application mode that does things for you: tool use, workflow automation, multi-step task execution. Distinguished from a chatbot (talks with you), RAG (searches for you) and a wiki (builds your knowledge).
The 1847 formalisation of steepest descent, and the pre-AI mathematical ancestor of every gradient-based learning rule — about 140 years before backpropagation put it to work in a neural network.
Wiener's 1948 treatment of control, communication and feedback as one subject shared by animals and machines. It predates the founding of AI by eight years and supplied much of its vocabulary.
Hebb's 1949 principle that neurons which fire together wire together, so learning is a change in connection strength. The basis for describing unsupervised learning in this course as Hebbian.

Weizenbaum's 1966 program that simulated a psychotherapist by matching patterns in the user's text and reflecting them back. The first well-known chatbot, and an early demonstration that fluency and understanding are separable.
A 1965 expert system, the forerunner of MYCIN, reasoning from hand-written IF-THEN rules with confidence factors and no training data at all.
Long Short-Term Memory (Hochreiter and Schmidhuber, 1997): a gated recurrent architecture that stops the error signal decaying over long sequences, making long-term dependencies learnable.

Sequence-to-sequence learning (Sutskever, Vinyals and Le, 2014): an LSTM encodes a whole sequence into one fixed-length vector which a decoder expands into the target sequence. Its fixed bottleneck is what attention removed.

The 2014 mechanism (Bahdanau, Cho and Bengio) letting a decoder soft-search the relevant parts of the source for each output word, instead of reading one fixed summary vector. The direct ancestor of self-attention.
Dosovitskiy and colleagues, 2020/21: a pure Transformer applied directly to sequences of image patches, with no convolution — the clearest evidence that the Transformer is a general architecture.
Devlin and colleagues, 2018. A Transformer that reads in both directions and is built for understanding tasks, sitting alongside GPT at the point where the Transformer became the standard for NLP.
Hinton, Osindero and Teh, 2006. Greedy layer-wise pretraining made deep networks trainable again and is where deep learning restarts after the 1980s stall.
A 1999 hand-designed local image feature, typical of the pre-deep-learning state of the art in which a human designed the features and a classifier such as an SVM did the rest.

For any continuous function on a closed bounded region and any tolerance, there exists a one-hidden-layer feedforward network with finitely many neurons approximating it uniformly. Cybenko 1989 for the sigmoid, Funahashi 1989, Hornik 1991. It establishes capacity, not trainability.

The design choices — skip connections, functional links, convolution, architecture — that make good solutions reachable by training. Since expressivity is abundant and trainability scarce, this is where the real leverage sits.

Pao, 1995. A network augmented with explicit nonlinear transforms of its inputs (polynomial, radial-basis, trigonometric), giving high expressivity at shallow depth when the useful features are known in advance.

The 2015 finding that beyond roughly 20-30 layers a deeper network fits worse than a shallower one, on the training set as well as validation. An optimisation failure rather than overfitting, and the problem the residual connection was invented to solve.

A shortcut that adds a block's input back to its output, so the block learns the residual F(x) = H(x) - x and outputs H(x) = F(x) + x. It lets the block refine rather than re-create, and makes identity mapping available by construction.

He, Zhang, Ren and Sun, 2015. A network of residual blocks, trainable to 152 layers and beyond, whose twelve-page paper became the most cited of the twenty-first century and whose block is now the standard backbone across vision and beyond.

The typical length of the paths that actually carry gradient during training. In a 110-block residual network it is 10 to 34 blocks, far less than the nominal depth — which is the sense in which ResNets behave like ensembles of shallow networks.
The step size that multiplies the gradient in the update rule. A hyperparameter, set before training: too small and training crawls, too large and the step overshoots.

The calculus rule for differentiating a composition, and the mechanism of backpropagation: it assembles the derivative of the loss with respect to any weight from a product of local derivatives, so one backward sweep gives every gradient.
The forward pass computes activations layer by layer to produce the prediction and hence the loss; the backward pass computes the gradients of that loss with respect to every weight.

The real shape of a network's loss: high-dimensional, full of local minima and saddle points, nothing like the bowl in the diagram. Gradient descent settles in a local minimum that in high dimensions is usually good enough.

An autoencoder trained to reconstruct a clean input from a deliberately corrupted copy, so the learned features must be robust rather than a memorised copy. The same idea sits at the heart of diffusion models.

The single fixed-length vector through which a pre-attention encoder-decoder had to squeeze a whole input. Attention removed it by letting the decoder weigh a sequence of encoder states per output element.
The 1980s ancestor of the autoencoder: a network trained to reproduce its own input, whose bottleneck hidden layer turned out to hold a useful learned representation.
The attention in a Transformer decoder that attends to the encoder's representations, as against self-attention, which relates a sequence to itself.

The multilayer perceptron inside each Transformer block — up-projection, ReLU, down-projection — applied to each token separately. It holds roughly two thirds of the parameters and acts as a key-value memory storing facts.
The packing of far more concepts than there are dimensions into one vector space, as overlapping nearly-orthogonal directions. It is why a single neuron does not correspond to a single concept.
A wide, mostly-inactive re-encoding of a model's activations, used to pull superposed concepts apart so they can be interpreted individually.

The two directions every generative model involves: TO maps data to a simple distribution, FRO maps back. Generation always uses FRO; TO exists only to create a supervised task with known targets. TO sets the homework; FRO learns to solve it backwards.
Evidence Lower Bound, the VAE's training objective. It splits into a reconstruction term keeping the output close to the input and a regularisation term keeping the latent close to the simple prior.
Generation steered by a condition such as a text embedding. The prompt is where to navigate; the PRNG is which possibility — which is why the same prompt gives a different image each time.

The three senses of the 'I': human-like (Turing's imitation game), advantageous information of strategic or tactical value (military, business), and an optimal solution path for a hard problem (computational, digital). Flagged in class as an exam notice in exactly those words.

One weight per incoming connection plus one bias per neuron. Inputs are given data and hyperparameters are fixed in advance, so neither counts. A two-input neuron therefore has three parameters; a layer of three neurons on four inputs has fifteen.

The geometric reading of a perceptron: a line, plane or hyperplane of one dimension fewer than the data, positioned by the weights and bias. Machine learning is then adjusting the parameters of those partitions until the data separate accurately.

Two ways a partition can misclassify, both errors but with different costs. A civil court minimises false positives; a military command minimises false negatives. No placement of the boundary eliminates both, so the threshold is a judgement about which error you can least afford.

A hard step has no useful derivative, so gradient descent has nothing to follow. Smoothing it with a sigmoid makes the model differentiable and therefore learnable, and turns rigid verdicts into graded probabilities.

The similarity measure attention is built on: it reports how congruent two vectors are, how far they point the same way. Each query is matched against every key by a dot product, and those scores become the weights that mix the value vectors.

Form, feeling, perception, mental formations and consciousness — the Buddhist list the lecturer draws the five elements of the Intelligent Being loosely from. Lecturer colour rather than deck material, but a useful handle on a list that is examinable.
